description: We are DeepKore, three friends from Málaga who like taking things apart to see how they work, from C code to AI. We are at the start of our journey, so we learn by building: we split the work, test ideas fast and keep what really works. We value curiosity, honesty and a good laugh when the code breaks at 3 a.m. Space Apps is our chance to learn from mentors, meet people who love space as much as we do, and turn open data into something useful.
summary: DeepKore is a free web app that helps rainfed farmers choose the crop rotation that protects their soil, and prepare before climate risks arrive. The farmer picks their field on a map, says what they grow today and what matters most: water, soil health, erosion or income. DeepKore downloads 25 years of NASA POWER daily data (2001-2025) for that point and computes a week-by-week calendar of frost, extreme heat and heavy rain, each crop’s water need (FAO-56), and the weeks when heavy rain falls on bare soil. It ranks the current rotation against the best alternatives and explains each one: why, evidence, benefits, data gaps and risks to check with a local agronomist. A what-if simulator shows how the ranking changes with less rain or more heat, and every number shows its source. The data correctly shows the 2022-23 drought as the driest season in 25 years at our pilot field in Antequera (Málaga, Spain). There, replacing sunflower with lentil raises the score from 42 to 68: more soil protection, less erosion, higher net margin. NASA data is global; in 48 hours we piloted it in Andalucía. DeepKore supports the farmer; it never replaces the agronomist.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

DeepKore answers the "Field Shift" question for one concrete user: a rainfed farmer who wants to know whether to keep their current crop rotation or change it. It compares at least three rotations, including the current one, and for each it shows why it is suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the data gaps and the risks that need a local check.

HOW IT WORKS

1. My field. Pick a point in Andalucía on the map (or use the pilot field in the Vega de Antequera, Málaga), set the field size, choose what you grow now and move four priority sliders: water, soil health, erosion and income.

2. Risk calendar. 52 weeks with the chance of frost (minimum < 0 °C), extreme heat (maximum ≥ 35 °C) and heavy rain (≥ 20 mm/day), computed as the share of the last 25 years in which that week had at least one such day; root-zone soil wetness now compared with the usual value; and the erosion window (heavy rain while the soil is bare).

3. Compare rotations. The current rotation and the three best alternatives, ranked by total = Σ(score × weight) / Σ(weights). Each card shows the crop sequence, why, evidence, benefits, gaps, risks, confidence, net margin and the difference with the current rotation.

4. What-if simulator. Rain from −40 % to +20 % and temperature from +0 to +3 °C re-run the same scoring and re-order the ranking (labelled "Simulated scenario", not a forecast).

5. Data & Limits. Every source with link, version, variables, resolution, licence and limits, plus a check against the 2022–23 drought.

SCORES (0–100)

- Water: rain in each crop's growing months ÷ crop water need (Kc × ET0, FAO-56).

- Erosion: 1 − share of heavy rain that falls while the soil is bare.

- Risk resilience: 1 − chance of each crop's main hazard in its sensitive weeks.

- Soil health: legume years and crop diversity.

- Income: net margin per hectare before CAP subsidies (Spanish Ministry of Agriculture, ECREA, Andalucía rainfed, 2018–2020).

VALIDATION

At the pilot field, rain from October 2022 to April 2023 was 193 mm against a usual 354 mm; spring 2023 (61 mm) was the driest of 25 years. The data shows the known 2022–23 drought clearly. There, replacing sunflower with lentil raises the score from 42 to 68 and the net margin from about 46 to 361 €/ha per year. 28 automated tests check scoring, ranking and the data contract.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Turns open NASA data into plain-language answers a farmer can use on a phone, free and without login.

- Shows the trade-offs (e.g. more soil protection vs. income) instead of a single "right" answer.

- Helps farmers adapt to a changing climate: protect the soil before the storms and see which rotation holds up with less rain or more heat.

- Every number is traceable to its source.

WHY ANDALUCÍA

NASA POWER covers every point on Earth, so the data and the code are global. Crop calendars, crop rules and margins are regional, and in 48 hours we wrote and checked them for our own region. Andalucía is the pilot, not a limit of the method.

STATUS

Built: live NASA POWER download and in-browser computation for any field in Andalucía; risk calendar; erosion window; rotation ranking by the farmer's priorities; build-your-own rotation; Data & Limits page.

Simulated: what-if climate scenarios.

Next: other regions worldwide; pilot with farmers and cooperatives in Málaga; add GPM IMERG, SMAP and NASADEM for finer resolution; CAP eco-scheme rules; irrigated fields.

LIMITATIONS

One NASA POWER cell is tens of kilometres wide; risks come from past years; no soil analysis or local prices yet; some crop-calendar values still need agronomist review. Decision support only: always check with your local agronomist.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript static web app; Leaflet (maps); Chart.js (charts); Web Worker for in-browser computation; Node.js data pipeline; GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/euZAPUS/deepkore

USE OF AI

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used by the team to write most of the web app and data pipeline code, tests, documentation and slides. Every change was reviewed, run and tested by the team; the full log is in AI_USAGE_LOG.md in the repository. While building, AI generated placeholder (MOCK) data to design the screens; it is kept only in data/mock/, is labelled MOCK and is never shown in the public app. Rotation texts were drafted with AI from the computed numbers and reviewed by the team. AI helped design the app layout, the logo and the slides. The 30-second demo video was made with the help of AI tools and is marked as AI-assisted. No NASA logos or branding are used.
